main.summary: The Great Learning sets out three guiding aims (making bright virtue shine, drawing close to the people - or, in Zhu Xi's reading, renewing them - and resting in the highest good) and eight steps, from investigating things to bringing peace under Heaven. Its claim is that everything rests on cultivating the self, and that personal growth reaches outward until the whole world is at peace.
main.translation:
The way of great learning lies in making bright virtue shine, in drawing close to the people (Zhu Xi read this as 'renewing the people'), and in coming to rest in the highest good. Know where to rest and you can be settled; settled, you can be calm; calm, you can be at ease; at ease, you can think carefully; thinking carefully, you can attain it. Things have a root and a branch, and affairs have an end and a beginning. To know what comes first and what comes later is to come close to the Way.
The ancients who wished to make bright virtue shine throughout the world first governed their own states well. Wishing to govern their states well, they first set their households in order. Wishing to set their households in order, they first cultivated themselves. Wishing to cultivate themselves, they first rectified their minds. Wishing to rectify their minds, they first made their intentions sincere. Wishing to make their intentions sincere, they first extended their knowledge. The extension of knowledge lies in investigating things.
When things are investigated, knowledge is complete. When knowledge is complete, intentions are sincere. When intentions are sincere, the mind is rectified. When the mind is rectified, the self is cultivated. When the self is cultivated, the household is in order. When the household is in order, the state is well governed. When the state is well governed, the world is at peace.
From the Son of Heaven down to the common people, all alike take cultivating the self as the root. It cannot be that the root is in disorder and the branches are in order. It has never happened that what one treats as weighty is made light, and what one treats as slight is made weighty. This is called knowing the root; this is called the height of knowing.
What is meant by 'making the intention sincere' is not deceiving oneself: to hate a bad smell as one hates it, to love beauty as one loves it - this is called being content within oneself. Therefore the noble person must be watchful over himself when alone. The petty person, at leisure and alone, does every kind of bad thing; then on seeing a noble person he slinks away, hiding his bad points and showing off his good ones. But people see him as though they saw right into his lungs and liver - so what does it gain him? This is what is meant by 'what is sincere within shows itself outside.' Therefore the noble person must be watchful over himself when alone. Master Zeng said: "What ten eyes watch and ten hands point at - how severe it is!" Wealth adorns a house, virtue adorns the person; when the heart is broad, the body is at ease. Therefore the noble person must make his intention sincere.
The Songs say: "Look at the bend of the Qi river, where the green bamboos grow lush and graceful. There is our refined noble man: as if cut, as if filed; as if carved, as if polished. How dignified and firm, how radiant and commanding! Our refined noble man can never be forgotten." 'As if cut, as if filed' refers to learning. 'As if carved, as if polished' refers to self-cultivation. 'Dignified and firm' refers to reverent caution. 'Radiant and commanding' refers to a stately bearing. 'Our refined noble man can never be forgotten' means that his way was rich in virtue and perfect in goodness, so that the people cannot forget him.
The Songs say: "Ah, the former kings are not forgotten!" Later noble persons honour what they honoured and cherish what they cherished; later common people enjoy what they enjoyed and profit from what they provided. That is why, though they have passed from the world, they are not forgotten.
The Announcement to Kang says: "He was able to make his virtue shine." The Tai Jia says: "He kept his eyes on the bright mandate of Heaven." The Canon of Di (Yao) says: "He was able to make his lofty virtue shine." All of these are about making oneself bright.
The inscription on the bath-tub of Tang says: "If you can renew yourself one day, then renew yourself every day, and again every day." The Announcement to Kang says: "Rouse the people to be new." The Songs say: "Zhou was an old state, but its mandate was new." Therefore the noble person uses every means to the utmost.
The Songs say: "The royal domain of a thousand li is where the people come to rest." The Songs say: "The little yellow bird chirps and rests in the corner of the hill." The Master said: "Even a bird knows where to rest. Can a human being be less than a bird?" The Songs say: "Solemn and majestic was King Wen; how he held, bright and unceasing, to the place where he rested in reverence!" As a ruler, he rested in humaneness. As a minister, he rested in reverence. As a son, he rested in filial piety. As a father, he rested in kindness. In dealing with the people of the state, he rested in trustworthiness.
The Master said: "In hearing lawsuits I am like anyone else; what we must do is make sure there are no lawsuits." Those who have no substance are not able to finish their pleas, and the people's will is greatly awed. This is called knowing the root.
What is meant by 'cultivating the self lies in rectifying the mind' is this. If the self is subject to anger, it cannot be rectified. If it is subject to fear, it cannot be rectified. If it is subject to fondness and pleasure, it cannot be rectified. If it is subject to worry and distress, it cannot be rectified. When the mind is not present, one looks and does not see, listens and does not hear, eats and does not know the taste. This is what is meant by 'cultivating the self lies in rectifying the mind.'
What is meant by 'setting one's household in order lies in cultivating the self' is this. People are partial towards those they love and are close to, partial towards those they despise and dislike, partial towards those they fear and revere, partial towards those they pity, and partial towards those they treat with arrogance and contempt. So there are few in the world who can like someone and still know his faults, or dislike someone and still know his good points. Hence the proverb: "No one knows how bad his own son is; no one knows how big his own crop is." This is what is meant by saying that if the self is not cultivated, one cannot set the household in order.
What is meant by 'to govern the state one must first set the household in order' is this. No one has ever failed to teach his own household and yet been able to teach others. Therefore the noble person, without leaving the household, completes the teaching of the state. Filial piety is how one serves the ruler; respect for elders is how one serves superiors; kindness is how one leads the multitude. The Announcement to Kang says: "Care for them as if for a newborn child." If one seeks it with a sincere heart, one may not hit the mark exactly but will not be far off. No one has ever learned to raise a child before marrying.
When one household is humane, a whole state rises to humaneness. When one household is courteous, a whole state rises to courtesy. When one man is greedy and perverse, a whole state rises in disorder. This is how the mainspring works. This is what is meant by 'a single word can ruin an enterprise; a single man can steady a state.' Yao and Shun led the world with humaneness, and the people followed. Jie and Zhou led the world with violence, and the people followed. When their orders ran against what they themselves loved, the people did not follow. Therefore the noble person first has it in himself and then asks it of others; he first lacks it in himself and then condemns it in others. It has never happened that someone who is not considerate in his own heart could make others understand. So governing the state lies in setting the household in order.
The Songs say: "The peach tree is young and tender, its leaves lush and full. This girl goes to her new home and will bring harmony to her household." Only when the household is in harmony can one teach the people of the state. The Songs say: "Good to elder brothers, good to younger brothers." Only when one is good to elder and younger brothers can one teach the people of the state. The Songs say: "His bearing is without fault, and sets the four quarters right." When he is worthy of imitation as father, son and brother, then the people imitate him. This is what is meant by 'governing the state lies in setting the household in order.'
What is meant by 'bringing peace to the world lies in governing one's state' is this. When those above treat the aged as the aged should be treated, the people rise to filial piety. When those above treat elders as elders should be treated, the people rise to respect for elders. When those above take pity on orphans, the people do not turn their backs. This is why the noble person has the way of the measuring square. What you dislike in those above, do not use in directing those below. What you dislike in those below, do not use in serving those above. What you dislike in those ahead of you, do not use in leading those behind. What you dislike in those behind you, do not use in following those ahead. What you dislike on the right, do not pass on to the left. What you dislike on the left, do not pass on to the right. This is called the way of the measuring square.
The Songs say: "Joyful is the noble lord, parent of the people." To like what the people like and to dislike what the people dislike - this is what is called being the parent of the people. The Songs say: "Steep is that southern hill, its rocks rising sheer. Mighty is Master Yin; the people all look to you." Those who hold a state must not fail to be careful; if they go astray, they will be cut down by the whole world.
The Songs say: "Before the Yin lost the multitude, they could stand as equals to the Lord on High. Take Yin as your mirror; the great mandate is not easy to keep." This means: win the multitude and you win the state; lose the multitude and you lose the state. Therefore the noble person first takes care over virtue. Where there is virtue there are people; where there are people there is land; where there is land there is wealth; where there is wealth there is use. Virtue is the root and wealth is the branch. If you treat the root as outside and the branch as inside, you will make the people quarrel and teach them to plunder. So when wealth is gathered, the people scatter; when wealth is scattered, the people gather. In the same way, words that go out in a wrong spirit come back in a wrong spirit, and goods that come in by wrong means go out by wrong means.
The Announcement to Kang says: "The mandate does not stay fixed." This means that if you follow the good you gain it, and if you do not you lose it. The Book of Chu says: "The state of Chu does not treat anything as a treasure; it treats goodness as its treasure." Uncle Fan said: "A man in exile has no treasure; he treats humaneness and love of his parent as his treasure."
The Oath of Qin says: "If I had but one minister, sincere and steadfast, with no other skill, but with a heart of great breadth, able to take others in - when others have a skill, he regards it as his own; when others are accomplished and wise, he loves them in his heart, more than his mouth can say. Truly able to take them in, he could protect my sons and grandsons and my black-haired people, and they would indeed benefit! But if, when others have a skill, he is jealous and hates them; when others are accomplished and wise, he opposes them and keeps them from advancement; truly unable to take them in, he could not protect my sons and grandsons and my people, and they would indeed be in danger!" Only the humane person can banish such a man, exiling him to the barbarians in the four quarters and refusing to let him live in the Middle Kingdom. This is what is meant by 'only the humane person is able to love people and to hate people.' To see a worthy person and be unable to promote him, or to promote him and be unable to put him first, is slackness. To see a bad person and be unable to remove him, or to remove him and be unable to send him far away, is a fault. To like what people hate and hate what people like is called going against human nature, and disaster is sure to reach one's own person. Therefore the noble person has a great way: he gains it through loyalty and trustworthiness, and loses it through pride and extravagance.
There is a great way to produce wealth: let those who produce it be many and those who consume it few, let those who make it be quick and those who use it be unhurried, and wealth will always be sufficient. The humane person uses wealth to enhance himself; the inhumane person risks himself to enhance his wealth. It has never happened that a ruler loved humaneness and his subjects did not love righteousness; that they loved righteousness and his affairs did not reach completion; or that the treasuries and storehouses in such a state were not truly his.
Meng Xianzi said: "One who keeps a team of horses does not concern himself with chickens and pigs. A family that cuts ice for its own use does not keep cattle and sheep. A house of a hundred chariots does not keep an official who piles up taxes. Better to have a thief among its officials than an official who piles up taxes." This means that a state should not treat profit as profit, but treat righteousness as profit. One who heads a state or a family and devotes himself to wealth and revenue must have been led to it by a petty person. He thinks that man is good and employs the petty person to run the state or family, and disasters and harms arrive together; even if good people appear, they can do nothing about it. This again means that a state should not treat profit as profit, but treat righteousness as profit.

keyLines.line: 大學之道，在明明德，在親民，在止於至善
keyLines.en: The way of great learning lies in making bright virtue shine, in drawing close to the people (Zhu Xi: renewing the people), and in coming to rest in the highest good.
keyLines.note: The master outline of the whole text, the 'three guiding aims': to bring out one's own luminous virtue, to help the people renew themselves for the better, and to arrive at the state of perfect goodness. Zhu Xi read 「親民」 (literally 'be close to the people') as 「新民」 ('renew the people').

keyLines.line: 知止而後有定，定而後能靜，靜而後能安，安而後能慮，慮而後能得
keyLines.en: Know where to rest and you can be settled; settled, you can be calm; calm, you can be at ease; at ease, you can think carefully; thinking carefully, you can attain it.
keyLines.note: The order of learning. Once you know your goal, your purpose becomes fixed; then the mind grows still and at ease, thought becomes thorough, and in the end you achieve something.

keyLines.en: Those who wish to govern their state must first set their household in order.
keyLines.note: One link in the chain of the 'eight steps': to govern a state you must first order your family. The steps before it (cultivating oneself, rectifying the mind, making the intention sincere, extending knowledge) are inner work, while 「平天下」 (bringing peace under Heaven) is the outer fulfilment.

keyLines.en: From the Son of Heaven down to the common people, all alike take self-cultivation as the root.
keyLines.note: From the emperor to the commoner, self-cultivation is the foundation for everyone. This is the hinge of the eight steps: self-cultivation sits at the centre, reaching back to investigating things, extending knowledge, sincerity and rectitude, and forward to ordering the family, governing the state and bringing peace.

keyLines.line: 所謂誠其意者，毋自欺也
keyLines.en: What is meant by making one's intention sincere is not deceiving oneself.
keyLines.note: This explains 「誠意」 (sincerity of intention): do not deceive yourself, and dislike what is bad and love what is good as sincerely as one recoils from a foul smell or loves a beautiful face. For this reason the noble person is especially careful when alone (「慎獨」, being watchful over oneself in solitude).

keyLines.en: If you can renew yourself one day, then renew yourself every day, and keep renewing yourself.
keyLines.note: Quoted from the inscription on the bath-tub of King Tang, founder of the Shang dynasty (c. 1600-1046 BC). It expresses the spirit of daily self-renewal and echoes the 「新民」 (renewing the people) of the opening. It is one of the most quoted lines in the Great Learning.

keyLines.line: 心不在焉，視而不見，聽而不聞，食而不知其味
keyLines.en: When the mind is not present, one looks and does not see, listens and does not hear, eats and does not know the taste.
keyLines.note: Explaining 「修身在正其心」 (cultivating oneself lies in rectifying the mind): when the mind is pulled about by anger, fear, fondness or worry, it cannot be upright, and even the senses stop working.

keyLines.en: What you dislike in those above you, do not use on those below you.
keyLines.note: The substance of the 「絜矩之道」 (the way of the measuring square): treat people above, below and on either side as you would wish not to be treated yourself. Judging others by your own heart is the basic principle for bringing peace under Heaven, and it agrees with the 'reciprocity' (shu) of the Analects.

glossary.en: ming ming de - 'to make bright virtue shine'
glossary.note: The first 「明」 is a verb, 'to make bright'; 「明德」 is the luminous virtue that people have by nature.

glossary.en: qin min - 'to be close to the people' / 'to renew the people'
glossary.note: The old text, with the commentaries of Zheng Xuan and Kong Yingda, reads 「親民」, 'be close to the people'. Zhu Xi, following the Song thinker Cheng Yi, read it as 「新民」, 'renew the people', meaning to help them leave the old behind and begin anew. Wang Yangming, a Ming philosopher, held that it should still be read 「親民」.

glossary.en: zhi yu zhi shan - 'to rest in the highest good'
glossary.note: 「止」 means to settle and abide; 「至善」 is the most complete good. It is the end point that bright virtue and the renewing of the people are meant to reach.

glossary.en: ge wu zhi zhi - 'investigating things and extending knowledge'
glossary.note: Interpretations of 「格物」 have always differed. Zhu Xi took it to mean exploring the principles in things, while Wang Yangming took it to mean correcting the wrong in one's own thoughts. 「致知」 means taking knowledge to its fullest extent.
To stay careful and self-governed when alone and unobserved, without indulging or deceiving oneself. The Doctrine of the Mean also speaks of this.

「絜」 means to measure and 「矩」 is the carpenter's square for drawing right angles. 「絜矩之道」 is to take the measure of others' hearts by one's own, so that people above, below and on every side are treated fairly.

glossary.en: cheng yi, zheng xin - 'sincere intention, rectified mind'
glossary.note: 「誠意」 is to make one's intentions genuine and free of falsehood; 「正心」 is to keep the mind from being swayed to one side by emotion. Both are the inner work of self-cultivation.

main.background: The Great Learning (Daxue) was originally the forty-second chapter of the Book of Rites (Liji), traditionally attributed to Zengzi, a disciple of Confucius, or to his followers. The Cheng brothers of the Northern Song dynasty (960-1127) held it in high regard. In the Southern Song (1127-1279) Zhu Xi grouped it with the Analects, Mencius and the Doctrine of the Mean as the 'Four Books', rearranged its chapters and wrote a supplementary section on 'investigating things and extending knowledge', producing his Commentary in Chapters and Verses. This copybook follows the order of the old text in the Book of Rites.
